title: The Code in the Iron Box

pages.text: Miss Tackie wrote a row of numbers on the board: 12, 5, 31, 8, 22. “What does this say?” “Nothing,” said Nathaniel. “It is only numbers.” “Exactly,” said Miss Tackie. “Today’s mystery is a set of numbers that some people have spent their lives trying to read.”

pages.text: “The story goes like this,” said Miss Tackie. “A man named Thomas Beale buried gold, silver and jewels in Virginia, in the United States, around 1820. In 1822, he left a locked iron box with an innkeeper, Robert Morriss. Years later, the box was opened. Inside were three papers covered in numbers.”

Years later, the box was opened.
Inside were three papers covered in numbers.”
pages.alt: An innkeeper opens an old iron box and finds three sheets of paper.

pages.text: “A pamphlet published in 1885 by James B. Ward told the story,” she went on. “Paper One said where the treasure was buried. Paper Two described what it contained. Paper Three listed the owners and their families. All three were written in code.” Dziedzom counted on her fingers. “Three papers, three secrets.”

pages.text: “Only Paper Two has ever been decoded,” said Miss Tackie. “It was a book cipher. Each number points to a word in a secret text, and you take the first letter of that word.” She wrote a short key on the board: Cats often seem tired. “What does 1 2 3 4 spell?” Nathaniel counted: Cats, often, seem, tired. “C, O, S, T,” he said. “Cost!”

pages.text: “For Paper Two, the key was the United States Declaration of Independence,” said Miss Tackie. “Number 115 meant the 115th word, and so on. It described a huge treasure: gold, silver and jewels. People say it weighed about three tons.” “Then the other two papers must use other keys,” said Dziedzom. “That is what many have tried,” said Miss Tackie. “Nobody has succeeded.”

pages.text: “So is the treasure real?” asked Nathaniel. “That is the second mystery,” said Miss Tackie. “Many experts doubt it. They point out problems: some words in the decoded paper were not used yet in the 1820s, we can find no clear records of Thomas Beale, and style analysis suggests the pamphlet’s author may have written it all.” Dziedzom frowned. “So it might be a hoax.” “It might,” she said. “But nobody can prove that, either.”

pages.text: “People have dug for the treasure, even in the twentieth century,” said Miss Tackie. “A dig in the late 1980s found only Civil War objects. Please remember: never dig on land that is not yours, and never trespass for a treasure hunt. Real discoveries are made with permission, by teams.” Nathaniel nodded. “Solving it on paper is safer.”

pages.text: At the end, Dziedzom wrote: Solved: Paper Two’s code. Unsolved: Papers One and Three. Open: is the treasure real? “And look,” said Miss Tackie, “what you have just learned: a code needs a key, and the key can be a book. Secret messages are a puzzle, but the best puzzles teach us how to think.” The end.
